draft.title: Choosing a display
card: data sorts things into groups, such as favourite sport or type of pet. A column graph or a pie chart suits it.
data is a count or a measurement, such as height or test score. A histogram, a stem-and-leaf plot or a dot plot suits it and shows how the values spread out.

A line graph suits data that changes over time, such as a town's rainfall each month. The line keeps the times in order and shows the trend. A histogram, stem-and-leaf plot or dot plot would lose that order.

To choose a display, first ask what type of data you have and what you want to show. Example: each student's way of getting to school (walk, cycle or bus) is categorical. A column graph shows how many students fall in each group.
draft.remember: Match the display to the data: groups, numbers or change over time.

a.q: Tamsin records the colour of each car that passes her school gate. Which option names the data type and a display that suits it?
a.why: Car colour sorts cars into groups, so it is categorical data and a column graph suits it. The option with a histogram names the data type correctly, but a histogram is for numerical data, such as counts or measurements, so it does not suit colours.
a.clue: Is a colour a group or a measurement?

b.q: The City of Greater Bendigo has the mean daily temperature for each month over three years. It wants to show how the temperature changed across that time. Which display suits this best?
b.why: The data is recorded over time and the aim is to show change, so a line graph keeps the months in order and shows the trend. Temperature is numerical, which makes a histogram or dot plot tempting, but both would lose the order of the months.
b.clue: Which display keeps the months in order?
